title.text: Before the first line of agent code

description.text: Build a map of the concepts first, then enter the real experiments with questions in hand. Seven opening chapters explain where agents come from, how models work and what they can't do, what an agent is made of, when not to use one, and how to judge completion with evidence.

intro.who-is-this-for.paragraphs.0.text: This course is for people who can write Python, want to understand how agents work, and want to build one themselves. You may have used chat apps like ChatGPT or DeepSeek, or written code with Cursor or GitHub Copilot in your editor, or called a model API once or twice, and still can't say what an agent adds on top of chat. You don't need to learn deep learning first, and you don't need any framework installed. You only need to be willing to read source code and to look closely at what a single request actually sends.

intro.who-is-this-for.paragraphs.1.text: After the native foundations and the units that follow, you should be able to do these things: hand-write a tool calling loop that uses no framework; read the key fields in a request and a response; write a task's acceptance criteria in advance and check them with a program; decide whether a requirement calls for a fixed flow or for letting the model choose the next step; and, when you use a framework later, say what it does for you.

intro.who-is-this-for.paragraphs.2.text: This course does not teach model training and does not derive the model's internal structure. Here the model is a component you call by the rules. The course is about the program around that component: how it organizes requests, runs tools, limits permissions, and records evidence. Retrieval, frameworks, and multi-agent systems are all covered. They are built on the same native mechanisms, so switching frameworks doesn't mean starting over.

intro.learning-loop.title.text: Every lesson uses the same learning loop

intro.learning-loop.paragraphs.0.text: Every experiment follows the same order: predict first, then run, then check and explain against the record, and finally change just one condition for a comparison. If you look at the result first and explain it afterward, you can almost always invent a reason that sounds right. If you write the prediction first, the places where your understanding is off show up.

intro.learning-loop.paragraphs.1.text: Take the "Add two numbers" exercise in {{lesson:tool-selection}} as an example. Before you click Run, write down whether you think it will call a tool, which one, with what arguments, and how many model requests it will send in total.

intro.learning-loop.item-1.text.text: Predict: does this task need a tool? If so, which tool is the first call and what are its arguments? Write it as a sentence the record can disprove.

intro.learning-loop.item-2.text.text: Run: pick one specific exercise, run it once, and keep this round's record.

intro.learning-loop.item-3.text.text: Check: in the record, connect the call the model proposed, the result Python returned, and the next round's request.

intro.learning-loop.item-4.text.text: Explain: say in your own words why there is a next round, and which event holds the evidence for each conclusion.

intro.learning-loop.item-5.text.text: Compare: change just one condition and run again, for example only the numbers in the question. Don't change the model, the prompt, and the tools at the same time.

intro.why-predict-first.title.text: Why you must write the prediction first

intro.why-predict-first.summary.text: Writing your expectation first exposes gaps in your understanding; an explanation after the fact can almost always justify itself.

intro.why-predict-first.paragraphs.0.text: When you explain after seeing the result, it's easy to feel "of course it works that way." The result is already in front of you, and your brain automatically weaves it into a plausible story. Writing a prediction fixes your understanding before you see the result and gives the result a chance to contradict it.

intro.why-predict-first.paragraphs.1.text: A good prediction is specific enough for the record to disprove. "It will call a tool" is too vague and is almost always right. "Round 1's response will contain 1 tool call, to the addition tool, with arguments 19 and 23" is different: if even one detail in the record doesn't match, you know where your understanding was off.

intro.why-predict-first.paragraphs.2.text: A wrong prediction is actually a gain, for example "I thought it would check the time first, but it just answered." Follow that gap back into the request and you will often find the model never received the time tool's definition, or that the question didn't make clear it needed the current time. Findings like this are worth writing into your learner notes.

intro.quiz-one-change-at-a-time.one-chan.text: You switched the model and changed the prompt at the same time, ran again, and the answer got clearly better. What does this comparison show?
It can't show that. The prompt also changed, so all of the improvement could come from the prompt.
It can't show that either. With two conditions changed together, their effects can't be separated.
Only that this combination did better in this run
Correct. To know which condition did the work, change one at a time, and run several times.
When two conditions change together, the difference can't be attributed to either one. And a difference from a single run may be nothing more than random variation.

intro.evidence-over-result.title.text: Why look at evidence, not just the result

intro.evidence-over-result.paragraphs.0.text: From the final answer alone you can't tell whether it was looked up, miscalculated, or made up, so you have to go back to the run evidence. Suppose you ask a coding agent to fix a failing test, and it replies at the end: "Fixed. All tests pass." That sentence could have three origins. It really ran the tests and the output shows all passing. Or it ran them but only ran some, or misread the output. Or it never ran them and just wrote the most common ending for this kind of task. In all three cases the final sentence can be word for word the same.

intro.evidence-over-result.paragraphs.1.text: If you have used tools like Claude Code or Cursor, you have probably seen what they look like at work: a terminal or sidebar lists, one by one, which file was read, which lines were changed, what command was run, and what the command printed. To judge whether "all tests pass" is true or false, look in that trail for the test command and its output. The explanation the model writes in its answer doesn't count, because that explanation is also text the model generated.

intro.evidence-over-result.paragraphs.2.text: This platform records each run in more detail: the request, the response, the tool call, the tool result, the final answer, and the end are each an event. To check a conclusion, first find the tool result that produced it and confirm the values match. Then confirm that the next round's request carried that result to the model. Only when all three line up does the conclusion have support.

intro.evidence-over-result.paragraphs.3.text: Evidence also has limits. One record proves only what happened this time; model output is random, and next time it may take another path. A record can prove a tool was executed, but not that the tool itself was written correctly. It can prove the answer used the result, but not that the task's goal was set sensibly. Later lessons deal with each of these questions.

intro.final-answer-is-not-proof.claim.text: If the final answer is right, the agent did it right.

intro.final-answer-is-not-proof.correcti.text: A right answer may have been looked up, or it may have been a lucky guess. To confirm it did what was asked, check whether the tool really ran, where the arguments came from, and whether the result went into the next round's request. A lucky guess can fall apart with a different input.

intro.finish-line.title.text: How to tell you're ready to continue

intro.finish-line.paragraphs.0.text: If you can point to where the evidence is, and can still explain the process with a different input, you can move on. Take tool calling: knowing the final answer is 42 isn't enough. You should be able to point to the tool name, the arguments, the execution result, and the place where that result enters the next round's request. After running again with different numbers, you should still be able to explain why the process still holds.

intro.finish-line.paragraphs.1.text: You don't have to read all seven intro chapters in one sitting. The next three chapters give background: where agents came from, how models work, and what models can't do. The chapters "What an agent is" and "Workflow or agent" cover agents themselves and when not to use one. The last chapter covers the learning path and how to use the lab bench. For chapters you already know, you can just do the end-of-chapter check.

intro.finish-line.paragraphs.2.text: The end-of-chapter check is your own record of how prepared you feel. The platform only saves the checkmarks and doesn't judge whether you have mastered anything. You can start the course even if you haven't memorized every concept, and come back to look things up when you get stuck. In the intro and in the lessons, a term is underlined the first time it appears; hover over it to see its definition.

intro.what-not-covered.summary.text: Training, model internals, and production deployment are not the focus. Here is where the course stops.

intro.what-not-covered.paragraphs.0.text: No training. Every model in the course is called through a provider's API, with its weights fixed. Pre-training and reinforcement learning get only the intuition, enough to see why the model behaves as it does.

intro.what-not-covered.paragraphs.1.text: No model internals. The attention mechanism gets one sentence; how it is computed doesn't affect your understanding of requests, tools, and the loop. If you want to go deeper, find dedicated material after the native foundations. By then you will know better which part you want to understand.

intro.what-not-covered.paragraphs.2.text: No promise of production-grade deployment. The platform binds to your own machine and is meant for one person to learn on. Lesson code runs in a local process and is not a sandbox. Running model-generated code requires an isolation plan first, and a later lesson covers that on its own.

agent-origins.what-agent-means.title.text: First, zoom in on the word "agent"

agent-origins.what-agent-means.paragraph.text: Anything that senses its environment and affects it through actions can be called an agent. By that definition, the air conditioner at home counts: it senses the room temperature and decides whether to cool or stop. The word is now used very broadly. Chat products, programming tools, and automation platforms all call themselves agents, so before discussing it, go back to its original meaning.

This definition doesn't care how smart an agent is. It only asks whether there is a loop of sensing and acting between the agent and its environment. Agents differ in what they base their actions on: a hard-coded rule, a remembered state, a goal to reach, or practices learned from experience. This chapter walks up that line and looks at what each level adds over the one before.

The concept of an agent is much older than large language models. Language models made one kind of agent, previously very hard to build, easy. But the places where earlier agents got stuck have not all gone away. You have to understand where they got stuck to see what today's LLM agents solve and what they don't. Many of the engineering practices in later chapters fill exactly those gaps.

agent-origins.capability-ladder.title.text: The capability ladder: each level fills a gap in the one before

agent-origins.capability-ladder.paragrap.text: Below we walk through some common devices and software. Each level up adds one more thing for the agent to consider when it decides on an action, and the last column explains why a move up was needed. In the classic textbook, "learning" can be combined with any of the first four levels; here it is placed last to make it easier to remember. The last row of the table is today's LLM agent, with Claude Code as the example. It isn't a new level from the textbook. It is a different way of supplying what the earlier levels needed people to provide.

agent-origins.capability-ladder.columns..text: What it bases its actions on
What the previous level can't do

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.0.1.text: Only the current perception, acting by "if ... then ..." rules

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.0.2.text: Air-conditioner thermostat: cool when the room is above the set temperature and stop when it reaches it; an early robot vacuum turns when it hits an obstacle

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.1.1.text: The current perception, plus a state it remembers

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.1.2.text: Many robot vacuums draw a map of the rooms in a phone app and remember which areas are cleaned; when the battery runs low they go back to charge, then resume from the areas not yet cleaned

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.1.3.text: A reflex agent only looks at the present: a robot that turns when it hits an obstacle doesn't know where it has cleaned, so some spots get cleaned several times and others are always missed

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.2.1.text: State plus a goal to reach, first asking "does this get me closer to the goal?"

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.2.2.text: Phone navigation: enter a destination and it searches for a route that gets there

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.2.3.text: With only state and no goal, it doesn't know which way to go; at the same intersection the right turn differs between going to the airport and going to school

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.3.1.text: Not just arriving, but picking the better one among several routes that arrive

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.3.2.text: In navigation you set preferences such as "avoid congestion," "fewer tolls," or "no highways," and it picks among routes by those preferences

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.3.3.text: A goal only separates arrived from not arrived; it can't compare two routes that both arrive

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.4.1.text: Adjusts its own way of acting based on the results of its actions

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.4.2.text: A short-video app adjusts what to recommend next from your records of watching to the end, swiping away, and liking

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.4.3.text: The rules, goals, and scoring of the earlier levels are all written by people in advance, and they can't keep up when the environment changes

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.5.1.text: Uses a language model to understand a task written in natural language, calls tools to act on the real environment, and decides the next step from each step's result

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.5.2.text: Claude Code: you say "this test is failing, fix it," and it reads the code, edits files, runs the tests, and decides the next step after seeing the test output

agent-origins.capability-ladder.rows.5.3.text: The rules, state, goals, and scoring of the earlier levels must be designed by people for each task, and a new task means starting over

agent-origins.ladder-everyday.title.text: Each level up needs someone to provide one more thing

agent-origins.ladder-everyday.paragraphs.text: Going up the ladder, each level up needs someone to provide one more thing. An air-conditioner thermostat needs just one rule and a set temperature. A robot vacuum has to remember a map and which places are cleaned, so someone must define how that state is represented and updated. Navigation needs someone to write "where to" as a goal a machine can use, and also a scoring method for comparing routes: is spending 10 more minutes worth saving 20 yuan in tolls?

At the learning level, what has to be provided is a learning signal. A recommender needs to know which video you watched to the end and which you swiped away after one second before it can adjust. Counted this way, what each level adds is the rules, the definition of state, the way the goal is written, the scoring standard, and the learning signal.

For a long time, AI research revolved around one question: can these things be written by people? And for the parts that can't be written, can the machine learn them itself? Rule systems took the first road.

agent-origins.quiz-ladder-level.ladder-l.text: A navigation app finds that two routes both arrive on time, so it picks the slower one because of your "fewer tolls" setting. Which level does this show?
Not quite. Reflex only applies rules to the current perception and doesn't compare several routes.
Close. A goal-based agent can find a route that arrives, but when two both arrive it has no standard for choosing.
Correct. Among routes that all arrive, it scores them by your preference and chooses.
Not quite. The preference is something you set in advance; it didn't adjust its way of acting based on results.
The utility level answers "which is better," and it needs a scoring standard to do that; here you set the standard.

agent-origins.symbolic-rules.title.text: Rule systems: reliable on closed problems, brittle on open ones

agent-origins.symbolic-rules.paragraphs..text: Rule systems are reliable on closed, well-defined problems and brittle on open ones. Their approach is to write knowledge as rules: a person first works out what to do in each situation, then turns it into conditions a program can run. A rule like "expense over 5,000 yuan needs manager approval" can be written once and then run reliably forever. The trouble comes with open problems, such as talking with people.

Many people have dealt with the early support bots. Here is a made-up example: a rule says "if the message contains 'refund,' reply with the refund process." You send "how do I get a refund" and it answers well. You send "I don't want a refund anymore, please hurry up the shipping," and it hands you the refund process anyway. The rule only matches the literal word. It can't read that "don't want a refund" means something else.

The only remedy is more rules: take another branch for "don't want a refund," treat "get my money back," "return and refund," and "can I get the money back" as synonyms, and so on. Every added rule has to be checked for conflicts with the existing ones and for which goes first. When the rules grow from dozens to thousands, nobody can say which one a given input will hit. Such a system works well in the situations its designer thought of, answers beside the point as soon as the input strays a little, and never says "I'm not sure."

Rule systems are still in use. The parts that can be written down clearly and must be 100% reliable still go to rules today: permissions, amount limits, format checks, approval flows. You will see later that a reliable agent keeps these rules in the program and hands only the judgments that can't be written down to the model.

agent-origins.eliza-by-hand.title.text: Tracing a pattern-matching program by hand

agent-origins.eliza-by-hand.summary.text: Four rules, three inputs: watch a rule system get the wording right and the meaning wrong.

agent-origins.eliza-by-hand.paragraphs.0.text: Below is a small program we made up in the style of early chatbots. It has four rules, matched in order, and it stops at the first match. One: if the input contains "I can't X," reply "What makes it hard to X?" Two: if it contains "I think X," reply "Why do you think X?" Three: if it contains "exam," reply "How many days until the exam?" Four: if nothing matches, reply "Can you say more?"

agent-origins.eliza-by-hand.paragraphs.1.text: Input "I can't understand recursion" matches rule one, and the reply is "What makes it hard to understand recursion?" Very natural. Input "I think the exam is too hard": rule two comes before rule three, so the reply is "Why do you think the exam is too hard?" That works too, but swap rules two and three and it would ask about the exam date instead. Input "I can't keep procrastinating" matches rule one, and the reply is "What makes it hard to keep procrastinating?" That misses the point completely.

agent-origins.eliza-by-hand.paragraphs.2.text: Three inputs expose three flaws of rule systems. It only sees the literal text, so it can't tell the "can't" of a resolution from the "can't" of a request for help. The order of rules changes behavior, and the more rules there are, the harder the order is to manage. And it has no way to say "I didn't understand"; the fallback fourth rule is just another stock phrase. ELIZA, published in 1966, was a program of this kind. Its best-known script played a psychotherapist, replying with keywords and rewriting templates, yet some people who chatted with it believed it really understood them, because people actively read meaning into vague replies.

agent-origins.eliza-by-hand.paragraphs.3.text: Swap in a language model and the same three inputs need no special rules: it can tell that "I can't understand recursion" is a request for help and "I can't keep procrastinating" is a statement of resolve. The price is that you can't check, rule by rule, what its answer was based on. That is one reason the later lessons keep asking you to look at evidence.

agent-origins.quiz-rule-breaks.rule-brea.text: Add one rule to the support bot above: "if it contains 'don't want a refund,' route to shipping inquiry." Does that solve its problem?
Yes, with this rule added it won't answer wrong anymore
It only patches this one sentence. New phrasings like "forget the refund" or "skip the refund for now" will keep turning up, and each needs another rule.
It fixes this sentence, but the rules keep multiplying, and order and conflicts must be handled
Correct. A rule system is reliable on the cases it anticipated and fails outside them, and the more rules, the harder they are to manage.
No, rule systems can't process text at all
Not quite. Rules can process text; keyword matching is exactly that. The difficulty is that open-ended phrasings can't all be written down.
Each rule covers only one phrasing the designer thought of; in open conversation, the phrasings nobody thought of always outnumber the rules.

agent-origins.knowledge-bottleneck.title.text: The knowledge acquisition bottleneck: rules have to be written one by one

agent-origins.knowledge-bottleneck.parag.text: A rule system can know no more than the part people are willing and able to write down. This is called the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. To make a system understand medicine, you have to ask doctors to put their diagnostic experience into words, and then have engineers translate it into rules. But doctors often can't say how they judge, and common sense is too vast to write out: "a tipped cup spills water," "schools are closed on weekends." Everyone knows these, and nobody thinks to write them down.
So no matter how finely rules are crafted, they cover only the cases someone thought of and wrote down. A rule system is often strong in a narrow domain and helpless outside it.

To break through this bottleneck you need a different source of knowledge, one where the machine learns from data and experience by itself. That is the idea of machine learning. There are many branches on this road. The ones with the biggest influence on today's agents are reinforcement learning and pre-training: one learns by trial and error, the other by reading.

agent-origins.reinforcement-learning.tit.text: Reinforcement learning: no rules, learn from rewards

agent-origins.reinforcement-learning.par.text: Reinforcement learning doesn't tell the machine what to do. It only says whether it did well, and lets the machine work out its own way by trial and error. Some things people can do but can't state rules for, such as a player's feel for the board or how to keep balance on a bicycle, and this approach fits there. Training a puppy is the same idea: you don't explain the technique, you reward it when it gets it right.

A reinforcement learning task is described by three things. The state is the situation the agent currently sees, the action is a choice it can make in that state, and the reward is a score the environment gives after the action. What the agent learns is a policy, the mapping from "which state, which action," and the goal is to maximize the long-run accumulated reward.

AlphaGo is the best-known example. In Go, the state is the board position, the action is placing a stone, and at the end of the game a win scores positive and a loss scores negative. It first learned from human game records, then kept improving through a huge number of self-play games, and in 2016 beat Lee Sedol 4 to 1. Recommendation can be described with the same three things: the state is the content you recently watched and swiped past, the action is what to push next, and the reward can be whether you watched it to the end.

The costs are also plain. First, it needs many trials: in Go the program can play itself, but real users won't sit through tens of thousands of trials. Second, once the reward is written off-target, the agent exploits loopholes: if the reward only counts "watched to the end," pushing shorter, more stimulating videos may be the easiest way to score. Finally, the learned policy belongs to this one task. AlphaGo can't play chess, let alone answer questions, and you can't tell it a new goal in a sentence.

agent-origins.reward-hacking.title.text: What happens when the reward is off-target

agent-origins.reward-hacking.summary.text: An agent optimizes the score you wrote down, not necessarily the goal in your head; in LLM agents this problem persists in a different form.

agent-origins.reward-hacking.paragraphs..text: A common phenomenon in reinforcement learning: the agent finds a shortcut to a high score without doing what you actually wanted. OpenAI published an example in 2016. In the boat-racing game CoastRunners, the researchers used the game score as the reward, and the score came mainly from hitting targets along the course. The agent learned to circle in a small patch of water and repeatedly hit a few targets that respawn. It caught fire, crashed into boats, and went the wrong way, yet scored higher than finishing the course normally, so it stopped trying to finish.

The agent was only optimizing the score that was written down. The goal in your head is "win the race" or "make the user truly satisfied," but what gets written down is a measurable score, and the gap between the two is where it finds loopholes.

LLM agents are no longer trained with rewards for each task, yet the same gap shows up in another form: the model is asked to complete a task, and the easiest thing for it to do is to say it has completed it. That is why later lessons require acceptance criteria to be written in advance and evidence to be checked by an independent program, rather than trusting what the agent reports. {{lesson:task-contract}} is devoted to this.

agent-origins.quiz-rl-parts.rl-parts.pro.text: Describe short-video recommendation of "what to push next" in reinforcement learning terms. Which of the following is the reward?

agent-origins.quiz-rl-parts.rl-parts.a.t.text: The videos you recently watched to the end and swiped away

agent-origins.quiz-rl-parts.rl-parts.a.f.text: That is the state, the situation seen when making the decision.

agent-origins.quiz-rl-parts.rl-parts.b.t.text: Whether to push a food video or a travel video next

agent-origins.quiz-rl-parts.rl-parts.b.f.text: That is the action, a choice available in the current state.

agent-origins.quiz-rl-parts.rl-parts.c.t.text: Whether you watched it to the end after it was pushed

agent-origins.quiz-rl-parts.rl-parts.c.f.text: Correct. The reward is the score the environment gives after the action, and the policy is adjusted according to it.

agent-origins.quiz-rl-parts.rl-parts.exp.text: The state is the situation seen, the action is the choice made, and the reward is the score received after the choice; together they describe a reinforcement learning task.

agent-origins.pretraining.title.text: Pre-training: swap writing rules for reading text

agent-origins.pretraining.paragraphs.0.text: Pre-training lets a model absorb knowledge from huge amounts of text on its own, getting around the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. The model reads a huge amount of text and does one thing only: predict the next token from the preceding text. This task needs no human-labeled answers; the articles, books, and code are themselves the answers. To guess accurately, the model has to learn grammar, common sense, facts, and even some reasoning steps, because all of these are hidden in the patterns of "what comes next."

agent-origins.pretraining.paragraphs.1.text: So knowledge doesn't have to be written as rules one by one, and no reward has to be designed for each task. It is absorbed into the model as a by-product of "predicting the next token." One model can know a little medicine, a little programming, a little history, and can also tell that "I want a refund" and "I don't want a refund anymore" are different things, which the support rule from earlier could not.

agent-origins.pretraining.paragraphs.2.text: Reinforcement learning hasn't left the stage either. After pre-training, a model usually goes through further training aimed at conversation and instructions, which often uses reinforcement learning: the model's answers are scored by human preference so it learns to follow instructions and to use tools more reliably. The next chapter explains how this step turns a model that only continues text into a model that answers.

agent-origins.pretraining.paragraphs.3.text: The limits are equally clear. The model's knowledge stops at the cutoff of its training data, and it is statistical patterns, not a lookup table, so it can misremember. It only outputs text and can't do anything by itself. These limitations are covered in detail in the chapter "What models can't do."

agent-origins.llm-agent.title.text: Three lines come together: the model becomes the decision core

agent-origins.llm-agent.paragraphs.0.text: An LLM agent lets the language model decide what to do next, and lets the program sense the environment, execute actions, and hold the rules. The earlier lines each had strengths and weaknesses: rule systems are reliable but brittle, reinforcement learning can learn but only does one thing, and pre-trained language models have broad knowledge and understand language but only generate text. An LLM agent combines them, each doing what it is good at.

agent-origins.llm-agent.paragraphs.1.text: In reinforcement learning terms, the language model plays the policy: it reads the current situation and outputs the next action. It doesn't need to be trained for this task; it can get started by reading a goal and tool definitions written in natural language. What used to require redesigning state, action, and reward can now start with a few sentences, and this is an important reason LLM agents have become popular in recent years.

agent-origins.llm-agent.paragraphs.2.text: Against the capability ladder, an LLM agent is not automatically at the top level. It can understand goals and weigh several options, but the "learning" level is usually achieved through context: the previous step's result is put into the next request, and the model's parameters are not updated. What it remembers, what it can do, and which rules it must not touch are still decided by the program around it. The chapter "What an agent is" calls that program the harness.

agent-origins.claude-code-today.title.text: What it looks like today: Claude Code as an example

agent-origins.claude-code-today.paragrap.text: Claude Code is a representative of the more mature LLM agents today: the language model decides the next step, and the surrounding program reads code, edits files, and runs commands. It is a coding agent from Anthropic and, according to the official documentation, can be used in the terminal, editor extensions, the desktop app, and the browser. You give it a task in one sentence, such as "the login test is failing, find the cause and fix it." It reads the relevant files, edits the code, runs the tests, and after seeing the test output decides whether to keep editing or stop. Depending on your permission settings, it can pause to ask for your confirmation before editing files or running commands.

Placed on the capability ladder, it adds three things. First, the task is written in natural language, with no rules to write and no reward to design for it; a pre-trained language model gets around the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. Second, it can act on the real environment: reading files, editing files, and running commands are really executed by the program, no longer stopping at suggestions in text. Third, it loops on observations: each step's test output is put back into the next request, and the next step follows the environment. This is a bit like the goal-based level, except that the goal is written in one sentence.

The old sticking points haven't all disappeared. It makes mistakes: it edits the wrong place, misreads test output, or runs only some of the tests and says all pass. The old problem of an off-target reward also returns in a new form, for example changing the test itself to make it pass. It doesn't know conventions in your project that aren't written down; Claude Code reads the `CLAUDE.md` instruction file in the project at the start of a session, precisely to put those conventions into the context. What it may touch is decided by permission settings, not by its own judgment; the official documentation also reminds you to check the changes and commands it proposes before approving them.

So a mature LLM agent still needs verification and permission boundaries: after edits, check them with tests and code review, and get a person's approval before dangerous operations. Its features keep being updated, so check the product documentation for specifics. The later lessons start from a single model request in {{lesson:chat-request}} and build the minimal version of this machinery step by step.

agent-origins.quiz-claude-code-gain.clau.text: Compared with a language model that can only chat, what does Claude Code add?
Knowledge of everything that happened after the training cutoff
Not quite. The model's knowledge still has a cutoff; it can read your project files because the program puts their contents into the context through tools.
Running tests, reading the real output, and deciding the next step from it
Correct. Tools let it act on the real environment, observations go into the next request, and that is how the loop turns.
Code it has edited is guaranteed correct and needs no more checking
Not quite. It can edit wrongly and misread output; its changes still need to be checked with tests and code review.
It updates the model parameters after each task, so it gets smarter the more you use it
Not quite. Model parameters don't change from a single run; conventions it can remember have to be stored externally, such as in an instruction file, and then put into the context.
What it adds is tools and a loop: the program carries out actions and hands the observations back to the model. The model's own limitations are still there, so verification is still needed.

agent-origins.rules-are-obsolete.claim.text: With LLMs, rules and fixed programs are obsolete.

agent-origins.rules-are-obsolete.correct.text: LLMs replace "judgments that can't be written down," not rules themselves. Parts that must be 100% reliable, such as permissions, amount limits, and format checks, are still executed by programs today. In a reliable agent system, there are often more hard-coded program rules than model calls.

how-llm-works.summary.text: Tokens, next-token prediction, sampling, and chat templates: understand what happens behind one request.

how-llm-works.objectives.objective-1.tex.text: Explain tokens and the tokenizer, and know why both the context window and the cost are counted in tokens.

how-llm-works.objectives.objective-2.tex.text: Use keyboard word suggestions and "next-token prediction" to explain how an answer is generated one token at a time, and why it stops.

how-llm-works.objectives.objective-3.tex.text: Work through one sampling step by hand with a small probability table, and explain why "Regenerate" brings a different answer and what temperature changes.

how-llm-works.objectives.objective-4.tex.text: Tell base models from instruct models, and explain how a message list becomes one piece of text through the chat template.

how-llm-works.single-call.title.text: From chat box to one request

how-llm-works.single-call.paragraphs.0.text: At the API level, one question and one answer is one HTTP request: send your question to the model, and bring the answer back. The request body says which model to use and attaches a message list, usually a rule written for the model and your question. The response brings back an answer, a finish reason, and how many tokens this call used. When you send a line and get a reply in ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Doubao, or Kimi, from the user's side it is exactly this one round trip. {{lesson:chat-request}} has you send such a request yourself.

how-llm-works.single-call.paragraphs.1.text: If you have used chat apps like these for a while, you may have noticed a few things: clicking "Regenerate" on the same question changes the answer; the answer appears in pieces, and sometimes cuts off halfway; and after a conversation gets very long, some products suggest you start a new one. All of these can be explained by how the model generates text.

how-llm-works.single-call.paragraphs.2.text: This chapter goes only as far as you need to use it and judge it: tokens, next-token prediction, sampling, and chat templates. How the model computes internally is out of scope and doesn't affect your understanding of the requests and tools that follow. The numbers in the text are small made-up examples and are marked as such where they appear; real numbers are left to the usage fields in the experiments.

how-llm-works.tokens.title.text: Tokens: the unit the model reads and writes

how-llm-works.tokens.paragraphs.0.text: The unit the model reads and writes is the token, so the context window and the cost are counted in tokens, not in characters or words. Before text enters the model, a tokenizer cuts it into pieces, and each piece corresponds to an ID in the vocabulary. The model reads a sequence of IDs and writes IDs, which are finally turned back into text. Those pieces are the tokens.

how-llm-works.tokens.paragraphs.1.text: Tokenization can be understood as compression by common fragments. A common word is often a single token, and a rare word gets broken into pieces. For example, the Chinese phrase "函数式编程" (functional programming) might be cut into three pieces, "函数," "式," and "编程," while one rare character may take several tokens by itself. So "how many tokens is one Chinese character" has no fixed answer; with another model's tokenizer, the count for the same text can differ quite a bit.

how-llm-works.tokens.paragraphs.2.text: This has two direct effects on you. First, the context window is an upper limit on the number of tokens, and input and output share that quota. A made-up example: for a model with a 32,000-token window, if the input already takes 31,000, the answer has at most 1,000 left. Second, cost is counted in tokens, and input and output are often priced separately, with output usually more expensive. Chat app interfaces generally don't show these numbers; when you call through an API, the provider reports in the response's usage field how many input and output tokens this call used.

how-llm-works.tokens.paragraphs.3.text: Estimating tokens from character count gives only an order of magnitude. For exact numbers, rely on the usage reported in the response; where the provider doesn't report it, write "not reported" and don't pass off a local estimate as the number. In {{lesson:chat-request}}, you will read these two numbers in the response's usage field and can compare them with your own estimate.

how-llm-works.context-cost.title.text: Why multi-turn conversations get more and more expensive

how-llm-works.context-cost.paragraphs.0.text: Multi-turn conversations get more expensive because every round sends all the earlier messages again. The model doesn't remember what was said in the previous round (the chapter "What models can't do" covers this in detail), so when you hold a multi-turn conversation through an API, the input of every round the program sends contains the inputs and outputs of all the earlier rounds.

how-llm-works.context-cost.paragraphs.1.text: As an analogy, it's like reading out all the earlier meeting minutes from the beginning at every meeting. The request in round 3 contains the rule, the questions and answers of the first two rounds, and this round's question. What you newly wrote this round is only the last sentence, but billing covers the whole thing. The more rounds there are, the larger the share taken up by old messages. {{lesson:multi-turn-history}} works through it round by round with a set of made-up numbers, then compares them with the usage per round in the lab report.

how-llm-works.context-cost.paragraphs.2.text: How chat apps handle history internally isn't fully public; check product documentation. What you can see when using them: some products suggest starting a new conversation when it gets long, and later in a conversation they sometimes fail to use details you gave at the start. When you write programs against an API yourself, long conversations get more expensive and slower, and eventually hit the window limit. {{lesson:context-budget}} and {{lesson:context-compaction}} discuss what to keep and what to drop when you exceed the window; {{lesson:prompt-caching}} looks at how a provider reuses the unchanged beginning of a request to lower cost.

how-llm-works.quiz-third-round-input.thi.text: By round 3 of a conversation, the request's input tokens are far more than the one question you wrote this round. Where does the extra come from?
The model stored the first two rounds in its own parameters
Not quite. Model parameters don't change from a conversation; it sees the first two rounds because the program sent them again.
The program resent the rules, questions, and answers of the first two rounds together with the new question
Correct. The input token count covers everything sent in this one request.
The longer the answers, the higher the unit price in the next round
Not quite. The unit price doesn't change; what changes is that each send contains more and more.
The cost growth in multi-turn conversations comes from resending the history, not from a change in unit price.

how-llm-works.next-token.title.text: Next-token prediction: extending the text one token at a time

how-llm-works.next-token.paragraphs.0.text: A model writes an answer by next-token prediction: each step predicts only the next token. It looks at all the tokens so far and guesses what comes next; once it has one, it appends it and guesses the next. An answer grows this way, one token at a time.

how-llm-works.next-token.paragraphs.1.text: A phone keyboard's word suggestions are a ready-made analogy. Type "This weekend, let's go" and the suggestion bar pops up "eat," "hiking," and "shopping"; whichever you tap, it keeps suggesting from there. A language model does the same kind of thing, except it looks at the whole preceding text, not just the last few words, and its candidates come from the entire vocabulary. Each time a token is appended, it is merged into the preceding text and the next token is predicted. This way of generating, using the output it just wrote as the input for the next step, is called autoregressive.

how-llm-works.next-token.paragraphs.2.text: When does generation stop? There are three cases. The model writes a special stop token, meaning this piece is finished; this is a normal ending and the finish reason is usually `stop`. The output reaches the length limit set in the request and is forcibly cut off; the finish reason is `length`. The output hits a stop sequence specified in the request and the provider cuts it off; the finish reason is usually also `stop`. The "Set a tiny output limit" exercise in {{lesson:chat-request}} shows the second case.

how-llm-works.next-token.paragraphs.3.text: Several phenomena in chat apps can be explained this way. Answers appear in pieces because they are generated one token at a time, and the interface displays them as they are generated. An answer that stops mid-sentence may have hit the length limit, and some products offer a "Continue generating" button. Once the start goes off track, the rest tends to follow, because each step takes what was already written as its premise. As for how the model decides which parts of the preceding text to attend to while predicting, that is the attention mechanism, and this course doesn't need you to know how it is computed.

how-llm-works.whole-answer-first.claim.text: The model first works out the whole answer, then writes it out all at once.

how-llm-works.whole-answer-first.correct.text: At each step the model predicts only the next token, and what it writes immediately becomes the input of the next step. If the start goes off track, the rest tends to follow; when the length limit is reached, the answer stops mid-sentence because the rest hasn't been generated at all.

how-llm-works.sampling.title.text: Probability distributions and sampling: why the same question gets different answers

how-llm-works.sampling.paragraphs.0.text: Asking the same question twice gives different answers because every step of next-token prediction is a weighted random draw. In a chat app, clicking "Regenerate" on the same question brings an answer with different wording, and sometimes even a different conclusion. At each step the model gives a probability for every candidate token in the vocabulary, and then draws one of them to append.

how-llm-works.sampling.paragraphs.1.text: Think of it as a loaded die. Take "This weekend, let's go" again: the "eat" face has 60%, "hiking" a little over 20%, and the other candidates split the rest. Roll once per step, and whatever comes up gets appended. Most of the time the highest-probability one comes up, and occasionally another one does; once a single step differs, everything after it differs too.

how-llm-works.sampling.paragraphs.2.text: The sampling temperature in the request controls how loaded the die is. At low temperature, high-probability candidates dominate and answers are more stable; at high temperature, the probabilities are flattened, low-probability candidates are picked more often, and answers are more spread out. Some providers also offer another kind of parameter: cut off the lower-ranked candidates first and draw only from the top few. Most chat app interfaces have no temperature setting; when you call through an API you can set it yourself.

how-llm-works.sampling.paragraphs.3.text: Temperature 0 still doesn't guarantee identical output every time; the provider's implementation and parallel computation can introduce small differences. So one run is just one sample and can't prove that the model always answers this way. {{lesson:sampling-variance}} runs the same prompt several times and compares the actual differences between low and high temperature.

how-llm-works.sampling-by-hand.title.text: Working through one probability draw by hand

how-llm-works.sampling-by-hand.summary.text: Four candidates and a few made-up numbers: see how one draw decides what follows.

how-llm-works.sampling-by-hand.paragraph.text: The preceding text is "This weekend, let's go," and suppose the model gives these probabilities for the next token: "eat" 0.6, "hiking" 0.25, "shopping" 0.1, "bowling" 0.05. These numbers are made up, only for demonstration, and sum to 1; to keep the arithmetic easy, also assume each candidate is exactly one token.

If it always picked the highest probability, the result would always be "eat." If it draws by probability, it picks a random number between 0 and 1: 0 to 0.6 selects "eat," 0.6 to 0.85 selects "hiking," 0.85 to 0.95 selects "shopping," and 0.95 to 1 selects "bowling." If it draws 0.9, this step writes "shopping," and the rest of the passage unfolds in a different direction.

Temperature changes exactly this table. At low temperature, the "eat" segment gets longer and the other three get shorter, so rolling another candidate is harder; at high temperature, the four segments are closer in length, and rolling "shopping" or "bowling" is easier. The model first scores each candidate and then converts the scores into this table, and temperature acts during that conversion. The deep-dive block in {{lesson:sampling-variance}} works through that conversion in full with another set of made-up numbers, then compares it with real runs.

Two points follow from this example. Temperature adds no information to the request; it only changes how to choose among the candidates already there. The higher the temperature, the easier it is to write low-probability content, which includes both novel phrasings and wrong ones. A real model's candidates at each step are the whole vocabulary, thousands upon thousands, but the principle is the same.

how-llm-works.quiz-what-temperature-chan.text: If you raise the sampling temperature from 0.2 to 1.2, which statement is correct?
The model reads more material, so answers are better grounded
Not quite. Temperature adds no information to the request; what the model reads is exactly the same.
The candidate tokens' probabilities are flattened, and lower-probability wordings are chosen more often
Correct. Temperature only changes how to choose among existing candidates, so answers become more spread out.
Not necessarily. More spread-out means more novel phrasings, and also more wrong ones.
Temperature acts on "how to choose," not on "what is seen."

how-llm-works.base-vs-instruct.title.text: Base models and instruct models: why it "answers"

how-llm-works.base-vs-instruct.paragraph.text: What can answer questions is the instruct model; a base model that has only been pre-trained can only continue text. Give a base model "Please explain what recursion is." and it will likely continue with "Please explain what iteration is. Please explain what a closure is." because in the training text a sentence like that is often followed by a list of similar questions. It is doing what it was trained to do: continue with the most similar text.

Turning a base model into an assistant that can hold a conversation takes another round of training: show it many conversation samples of "a question and a good answer," then have people or programs score its answers, so it learns to write an answer after a question instead of more questions. The resulting model is called an instruct model, also called a chat model. The models you chat with in chat apps all belong to this type.

Underneath, an instruct model is still doing next-token prediction; it has just learned what should come next. So it is still affected by sampling, and it can still make things up. Following instructions is a probabilistic tendency, not a guarantee from the program. A line in the prompt like "never do X" can lower the probability that the model does it, but it can't block it completely the way a program's permission check can.

how-llm-works.chat-template.title.text: The chat template: how a message list becomes one piece of text

how-llm-works.chat-template.paragraphs.0.text: A message list has to be assembled by the chat template into one piece of text before the model can read it. A chat app shows a conversation as bubbles on the left and right; the API instead asks you to send a message list by role: `system`, `user`, `assistant`, and, when tools are used, `tool`. But the model reads one long string of tokens and has no concept of a "list." The chat template does the conversion in between: the provider's backend assembles the list into a piece of text with special tokens, using the format this model was trained with.

how-llm-works.chat-template.paragraphs.1.text: The assembly goes roughly in the order below. Each model's markers differ, and you can't see this step in the API, but it determines what the model actually reads.

how-llm-works.chat-template.item-1.text.text: Before each message, add a special token for "this role begins," followed by the message content and then an "end" marker.

how-llm-works.chat-template.item-2.text.text: Tool definitions are written into the text in the format the model expects, usually near the rules. To the model, tool definitions are also just text it reads.

how-llm-works.chat-template.item-3.text.text: All messages are joined end to end in order into one complete text, with every earlier round's questions and answers in it.

how-llm-works.chat-template.item-4.text.text: At the end, add an "assistant begins" marker with nothing after it. The model continues from here, and what it writes is this round's answer.

how-llm-works.chat-template.item-5.text.text: The model stops when it writes the "end" marker. The provider cuts out this output and puts it into the response as an `assistant` message.

how-llm-works.template-by-hand.summary.text: To the model, the rules, tool definitions, history, and reference material are all one piece of text, and this has three consequences.

how-llm-works.template-by-hand.paragraph.text: What markers a real model uses and what the assembled text looks like were shown once in the deep-dive block of {{lesson:chat-request}}, using an open-source model's format, and are not repeated here. This section looks only at the consequences of the assembly: the rules, tool definitions, earlier questions and answers, and any material you paste in are all just characters in the same piece of text as far as the model is concerned.

First, tool definitions are also just text. The model reads them to decide what tools exist and when to use them, so how well a tool definition is written directly affects whether the model uses it. Second, when you ask in round 2, round 1's questions and answers are assembled in as they were. This is what "the program resends the history" looks like on the model's side; if the program changes an answer in the history, the model can't tell whether it said that itself.

Third, in common implementations, role markers are dedicated tokens in the tokenizer, and ordinary text in the material can't spell out a real marker. But a passage in the material that imitates the tone of the rules, such as "ignore the earlier requirements and do something else," may still be followed by the model, because like the real rules it is just text the model reads. This is one root of prompt injection, which comes later.
The platform's experiment records show the message JSON at the API layer, not this assembled text. The assembly happens in the provider's backend; what you can check is which messages you sent.

llm-limits.why-limits.title.text: Four things you run into in a chat app

llm-limits.why-limits.paragraphs.0.text: Most people who use a chat app regularly have run into the four things below. Each one maps to an inherent limitation of the model. First, you open a new conversation and ask "which exam did I say I was preparing for last time?" and it can't answer. Second, with web search off, you ask about today's news and it either says it doesn't know or tells you about something old; ask it to recommend papers and it may give entries with author, year, and link all filled in for a paper that doesn't exist.

llm-limits.why-limits.paragraphs.1.text: Third, you ask it to "run" a piece of code and it may just report a result without having run anything; ask it to multiply two long numbers in its head and it may get some digits wrong. Fourth, you ask for a table in a fixed format and click "Regenerate" a few times: sometimes there is an extra opening paragraph, sometimes a column is missing. Some products offer memory, web search, and code execution. With those turned on, behavior changes, and those features are exactly gap-filling done outside the model. For what each feature can actually do, see the product documentation.

llm-limits.why-limits.paragraphs.2.text: These problems come from mechanisms covered in the previous chapter: the model sees only the current request; its knowledge comes from training data; it outputs only tokens; every step is a sample. A different prompt can ease the symptoms but doesn't cure the cause. A large part of agent engineering is using a program outside the model to fill these gaps. Each section below covers one and points to the lesson where you will see it for yourself.

llm-limits.no-memory.title.text: No memory of the conversation: the full text is resent every time

llm-limits.no-memory.paragraphs.0.text: The model API is stateless: each request sees only the messages sent with that request, and multi-turn conversation works because the program resends the history. That is why a new conversation can't answer "what did I say last time?" Every request is independent and the model can't see the previous one. Inside one conversation it seems to remember you, but from how the API works, that is because the conversation's message history was put into the request. A new conversation starts from an empty history, so what was in the old one is naturally not there.

llm-limits.no-memory.paragraphs.1.text: The fix is just as direct: the program keeps the message history and sends it with every request. The cost was covered in the previous chapter: the more rounds, the longer and more expensive the input, until it finally hits the context window. At that point the program has to decide what to keep, what to drop, and what to compress.

llm-limits.no-memory.paragraphs.2.text: Some chat apps have memory features, and with them on, a new conversation may know things you said before. The model's parameters don't change because of one conversation. Such features usually mean the product stores information outside the model and puts it into the request when needed; for what is stored and how it is retrieved, see the product documentation. {{lesson:multi-turn-history}} compares requests with and without history; {{lesson:context-budget}} handles the case where the window can't hold everything; {{lesson:persistent-memory}} stores information in a database and recalls it across runs.

llm-limits.knowledge-cutoff.title.text: A knowledge cutoff, and no view of your private data

llm-limits.knowledge-cutoff.paragraphs.0.text: The model doesn't know what happened after training, and it can't see private material that was never public. A program has to supply that information at request time. Asking about today's news fails because of the knowledge cutoff: the model's knowledge comes from training data, which was collected up to some point in time, and anything after that, such as today's news or a newly released library version, the model has never seen. The other kind it can't possibly know: a company's internal documents, or your own calendar and files, were never public, so no model could have read them during training.

llm-limits.knowledge-cutoff.paragraphs.1.text: With web search on, many products list which web pages they consulted, and answers can keep up with recent events. You can think of it as the search results entering the context the model can read in this request; see the product documentation for how it actually works. That is the fix: information the model needs but the training data lacks is supplied by the program at request time. You can put the material straight into the context, or give the model a tool so it can look things up when needed. The former is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation; the latter is tool calling.

llm-limits.knowledge-cutoff.paragraphs.2.text: There is one special case: the model doesn't know when "now" is. Its training data stops in the past, but every request happens today. A task that needs the current time either has the program write the date into the request, or provides a tool that reads the clock. In {{lesson:dependent-calls}}, the model first proposes a call that reads the clock, the program reads the real time of this run, and the model then continues the calculation with the hour and minute it got back. That is the second approach.

llm-limits.what-day-is-it.title.text: The model doesn't know what day it is

llm-limits.what-day-is-it.summary.text: Time is the most common piece of information that training data doesn't have. See how providers and programs each fill it in.

llm-limits.what-day-is-it.paragraphs.0.text: Ask a model "what day of the week is it today?" and it can only guess. Its training data stops on some day in the past, the request happens today, and the model has no way to know how long the gap is. Worse, it may not even be sure which day its own knowledge cutoff falls on; it can only infer it from the latest content in its training data.

llm-limits.what-day-is-it.paragraphs.1.text: The chat templates of some open-source models leave a slot in the `system` section for the knowledge cutoff date and today's date, and the caller fills in today's date. When a template has no such slot, your program has to fill the gap: write today's date into the system prompt, or provide a tool that reads the clock.

llm-limits.what-day-is-it.paragraphs.2.text: The two fixes differ in freshness. A date written into the prompt is fixed at the moment the request is sent. A tool is called only when the model actually needs it, and it returns the time at the moment of execution. Either is enough to work out "how many days until the end of the month." To record the exact moment something happened, the program should read the clock at execution time instead of asking the model to write a time.

llm-limits.quiz-record-the-time.record-t.text: An agent has to write "the moment this task was completed" into a to-do record. Which approach is reliable?
Ask the model to write a time in its answer
Not reliable. The model doesn't know what time it is, so the time it writes may be made up.
Write the date at request time into the system prompt and have the model copy it
Not enough. The date is only accurate to the day, and it is fixed at the moment the request is sent, not the moment the task finished.
Have the program read the clock when it writes this record
Correct. The time comes from the real clock at execution, without passing through the model.
Facts that need an exact time should be read by the program at execution time, not generated by the model.

llm-limits.hallucination.title.text: Hallucination: fluent is not the same as true

llm-limits.hallucination.paragraphs.0.text: A model can state unsupported content as if it were true: fluent sentences and a confident tone, but at odds with the facts or the material you gave it. This is called hallucination. Ask a chat app to recommend a few papers with links and it may give entries with title, author, year, and journal all filled in; you look them up and they don't exist, and the links don't open. It is common in code too: calling a function that doesn't exist in a library, or quoting a passage that isn't in the source material.

llm-limits.hallucination.paragraphs.1.text: Recall next-token prediction: at every step the model continues with the most likely next text. Asked to "recommend three papers," the most likely continuation is three well-formed citations, not "I'm not sure which ones exist." The model has no built-in step that checks facts first. Its training objective is to write plausible text. Plausible and true overlap most of the time, but not always.

llm-limits.hallucination.paragraphs.2.text: Hallucination is most likely when information is missing: the answer isn't in the context, so the model can only rely on vague impressions in its parameters, or simply fill in the blanks to fit the format. The first line of defense is to put real material into the context. The second is to require the answer to say which passage or which tool result it relies on. The third is to check with a program, for example verifying that a cited passage actually exists.

llm-limits.hallucination.paragraphs.3.text: These measures reduce hallucination; they don't eliminate it. Even with a tool, the model can misread the tool result, or invent a "tool return" of its own in the text. A made-up answer is often as confident as a real one, so tone tells you nothing. {{lesson:text-actions}} removes the stop sequence for comparison: the model may "write" a tool result in the tool's place. Whether that happens, and what it makes up, check in your own run record.

llm-limits.why-hallucinate.title.text: Why a model makes things up with a straight face

llm-limits.why-hallucinate.summary.text: Training rewards text that looks right, and "I don't know" is rarely the most likely continuation.

llm-limits.why-hallucinate.paragraphs.0.text: The objective of pre-training is to predict the next token. In the training text, a question is usually followed by an answer and rarely by "I don't know." So the model learns a tendency: when asked, write something shaped like an answer. When it doesn't actually have the information, the tendency is still there, and the result is a reply that is complete in form and empty in content.

llm-limits.why-hallucinate.paragraphs.1.text: Later conversation training teaches the model to admit when it is unsure, but only partly corrects the tendency. The people or programs that score answers often prefer specific, confident ones, too. The model's own judgment of "how much do I know" is also unreliable: it doesn't really know how many times a piece of knowledge appeared in its training data.

llm-limits.why-hallucinate.paragraphs.2.text: Another kind of hallucination comes from the continuation drifting off course and has nothing to do with missing knowledge: an earlier step samples a wrong word, and later steps keep making things up to stay consistent with it. This is also why long answers often contain more than one error.

llm-limits.why-hallucinate.paragraphs.3.text: In engineering terms: don't expect the model to notice that it is making things up. Put the evidence in the context, require the answer to point to it, and have a program or a person check that the evidence exists and really supports the conclusion.

llm-limits.quiz-unverified-citations.unv.text: A chat app has web search off. You ask it to recommend three related papers, and it gives titles, authors, years, and links. The conversation has no search results and no material from you. What is the most reasonable judgment?
They are probably all correct; the model has read a lot of papers
Not necessarily. It may have seen some of these papers, but details like titles, authors, and links are the easiest to invent convincingly. Without a source, check each one.
These entries have no source; some may be real and some fake, so verify each one
Correct. With no material and no search results in the context, these entries can only come from the model's continuation, so whether they are real has to be checked separately.
The more standard the format and the more confident the tone, the more trustworthy
Not quite. Made-up entries can be just as well formatted and just as confident.
Judge by the source: information can only come from the request content or a tool result. With neither, the conclusion has no basis.

llm-limits.text-only.title.text: Text-only output: saying "I ran it" is not running it

llm-limits.text-only.paragraphs.0.text: The model outputs only text. When it says "done," nothing has necessarily happened. Ask a chat app that can't execute code to "run this Python and tell me the output" and it may just report an output. That is text it predicted; no program ran the code. With slightly more complex code, the reported output can be wrong. Mental multiplication of big numbers is the same: every digit it writes comes out of next-token prediction.

llm-limits.text-only.paragraphs.1.text: To let a model actually do things, give it tools. The program attaches tool definitions to the request, telling the model there is a "run code" or "multiply" tool and what parameters it takes. If the model decides to use one, it writes a structured tool call proposal in the response, with the tool name and arguments. That is still only text. The program then reads the proposal, checks that it is allowed and the arguments are valid, actually executes it, and puts the result into the next request. Some chat apps offer code execution; with it on, you can see the code it wrote and the run output, and a calculation like big-number multiplication can be handed to code.

llm-limits.text-only.paragraphs.2.text: The later lessons follow this division of labor. {{lesson:tool-proposals}} looks only at what calls the model proposes and executes none of them; in {{lesson:tool-selection}}, Python executes calls against an allowlist and sends the results back to the model; {{lesson:fail-safely}} looks at how the program refuses when a call points to an unregistered tool or has invalid arguments. What can and can't be done is decided by the program, not by the model's wording.

llm-limits.unstable-output.title.text: Unstable output: the same request, different results

llm-limits.unstable-output.paragraphs.0.text: With the same request, the model's output can differ every time, so output that a program will read must be validated. You have seen this when clicking "Regenerate": ask for a table in a fixed format, and this time there is an extra opening paragraph, next time a missing column, or "three items" becomes four. The causes are sampling and the model's sensitivity to wording; rephrase the prompt and the result can change noticeably. In chat this is harmless. For output a program will read, it is a fault: downstream code expects a fixed structure and receives a paragraph of prose.

llm-limits.unstable-output.paragraphs.1.text: The fix has three layers. First, ask the model to output an agreed structure, then validate it against that structure with a program; reject what doesn't pass, or hand the error reason back to the model for one repair. That is the content of {{lesson:structured-output}}. Second, a correct structure doesn't mean correct content, so also check business rules: item counts, value ranges, whether the parts agree with each other. Third, a conclusion like "is this change effective?" can't rest on one run: run several times and change only one condition. That is the approach in {{lesson:sampling-variance}} and {{lesson:prompt-experiments}}.

llm-limits.unstable-output.paragraphs.2.text: Validation can guarantee format and rules, but not that the content is true; repeated runs show how large the fluctuation is, but can't remove it. That is why {{lesson:task-contract}} asks you to write acceptance criteria before you start: what output counts as done, and what evidence you judge it by.

llm-limits.limits-map.paragraphs.0.text: Put the four limitations side by side: each row is something the model can't do by itself and a program fills in. The later lessons mostly follow this table.

llm-limits.bigger-model-fixes-all.claim.text: Switch to a bigger, newer model and all of these problems go away.

llm-limits.bigger-model-fixes-all.correc.text: A stronger model usually hallucinates less and keeps formats more stable, but the four limitations come from how models work: the API is still stateless, the training data still has a cutoff, the output is still just text, and generation is still sampling. What the program has to fill in, it still has to fill in after a model swap.

what-is-agent.summary.text: Using Claude Code as the example, see how a model, context, tools, and a harness make up a system that can take action.

what-is-agent.objectives.objective-1.tex.text: Use "model + context + tools + harness" to say what an LLM agent is made of and what each part is responsible for.
