what-is-agent.definition.title.text: From answering questions to choosing the next action

what-is-agent.definition.paragraphs.0.text: In this course, an LLM agent is a system in which a language model chooses the next action based on the current context, a program executes the action and hands the result back to the model, and this repeats until the task is done or a stop condition fires. Claude Code is a ready-made example. In a project directory you ask it to fix a bug that makes a test fail. It usually reads the files named in the error, changes a few lines, and runs the test; if the test still fails, it reads the new error and keeps going, until the test passes or it stops to ask you. You can see the same process in coding agents such as Cursor and GitHub Copilot's agent mode.

what-is-agent.definition.paragraphs.1.text: Compare that with using a chat-only app. You paste the error into the chat app and it suggests a change; you copy the code, run the test, and paste the new error back. After a few rounds, you are the one who has been running tests and pasting errors the whole time. A coding agent hands that step to a program: the model proposes "run the tests," the program executes it, and the output goes back to the model. Both can use the same kind of model. The difference is who drives the next step, and whether a new observation comes in after each step.

what-is-agent.definition.paragraphs.2.text: The common shorthand is: agent = model + context + tools. The model makes decisions, the context determines what it can see, and the tools determine what it can do. The shorthand leaves out one thing: the layer of program that organizes the three, keeps the loop turning, and enforces the rules. This course calls it the harness.

what-is-agent.boundaries.paragraphs.0.text: Take an agent apart and you find four positions: the model, the context, and the harness are inside the agent; the environment is outside it. For a coding agent, the environment is your project directory, terminal, and tests, and the agent can deal with it only through observation and action.

what-is-agent.boundaries.paragraphs.1.text: Tools span several positions: a tool definition is written in the context for the model to see, the harness is responsible for executing the tool, and whatever the tool reads and writes belongs to the environment.

what-is-agent.boundaries.rows.0.1.text: Generates an answer from the context it receives, or proposes the next action

what-is-agent.boundaries.rows.0.2.text: That it can directly run local Python or read any file

what-is-agent.boundaries.rows.1.1.text: The rules, message history, tool definitions, and tool results provided in this one request

what-is-agent.boundaries.rows.1.2.text: That the model automatically knows anything that exists on disk

what-is-agent.boundaries.rows.2.1.text: Builds the request, validates arguments, dispatches tools against an allowlist, records events, limits the number of rounds

what-is-agent.boundaries.rows.2.2.text: That a requirement written in the prompt automatically equals what the program is permitted to do

what-is-agent.boundaries.rows.3.1.text: Provides real state and execution results, such as project files, test output, and the current time

what-is-agent.boundaries.rows.3.2.text: That a result the model describes is necessarily what happened in the environment

what-is-agent.harness.title.text: The harness: outside the model, inside the agent

what-is-agent.harness.paragraphs.0.text: The harness is the layer of program wrapped around the model that lets it do work reliably. The model only reads a piece of context and writes a piece of output. Turning the output into a real action, and turning the action's result back into the next piece of context, is done at every step by the harness.

what-is-agent.harness.paragraphs.1.text: In this course's terms, for an agent that fixes bugs the harness does the following. It first assembles the request, with the rules, the message history, and the definitions of tools for reading files, editing files, and running commands. After the response arrives, it reads the calls the model proposed and checks whether the tool name is on the allowlist and the arguments are valid. If so, it executes the call and writes the result back to the message history together with the matching `tool_call_id`. Then it decides whether to continue, for example whether the round limit has been reached. Every step is recorded as an event and kept as evidence. Claude Code can be set to ask you before it edits files or runs commands, and you choose to approve just this once or to allow it from now on. That step is also part of the harness: the model proposed an operation, and the program stops to ask you before executing it.

what-is-agent.harness.paragraphs.2.text: One way of putting it is very direct: the model is the driver and the harness is the car. The driver's skill comes from training; the car determines which road conditions the driver can see and which pedals can be pressed. In a harness you can trust, a lot of the code goes into constraints, checks, and error correction: which operations need human approval, how to retry after a failure, how to verify results.

what-is-agent.harness.paragraphs.3.text: The runner of every lesson on this platform is a minimal harness. Starting from {{lesson:tool-selection}}, you will see it grow, step by step, an allowlist, error handling, a round limit, and acceptance checks. Frameworks also do the harness's work; once you have learned the native implementation, you will see what code a framework writes for you.

what-is-agent.agent-as-policy.title.text: The same thing in reinforcement learning terms

what-is-agent.agent-as-policy.summary.text: The model corresponds to the policy, the context to the observation, and the tools to the action interface; the environment always stays outside the agent.

what-is-agent.agent-as-policy.paragraphs.text: The "Where agents came from" chapter used three words when it covered reinforcement learning: state, action, and reward, with the agent learning a policy. Map an LLM agent onto them. The model is the policy: it reads the current situation and picks the next action. The context is the agent's internal representation of observations and history. The tools define which observations the agent can read and which actions it can issue.

This mapping helps you see one thing: with the model held fixed, the most direct way to improve an agent is often to change the interface of observations and actions, not to swap in a smarter model. A coding agent that keeps looking for the cause in the wrong place may simply not have the full error message in its context. One that only gives suggestions and doesn't act may simply have no tool for editing files.

The mapping has limits too. The context is not the whole environment; it is only the part the program picked out and put into the request. A tool is not the environment either; the database, files, and clock behind the tool are. The environment changes on its own, out of the agent's control, so after every action you must observe again instead of assuming everything went to plan.

what-is-agent.quiz-who-executes.who-exec.text: A coding agent's model proposes a call to run the tests in its response. Have the tests run at this point?
Yes, a call in the response means it was executed
Not quite. The response contains only a tool call proposal, which is structured text.
Not yet; the harness still has to validate and execute the call
Correct. Execution happens in the harness, and the test output reaches the model only in the next request.
Partly; the model previewed the test results first
Not quite. The model has no access to the terminal; it sees only what the request gives it.
Proposing a call and executing a call are two steps, handled by the model and the harness respectively.

what-is-agent.context-parts.paragraphs.0.text: Each time the model decides something, all it sees is the context in this one request. It usually has five parts: the system prompt, the tool definitions, the user message, the model's earlier replies, and the tool results. The first two stay mostly unchanged over the whole task, like a fixed opening; the last three grow longer round by round as the loop runs, and together they are the message history.

what-is-agent.context-parts.paragraphs.1.text: Leave out any part and the agent breaks in a different way. Without tool definitions, the model doesn't know any tools are available, so it answers from impressions, and as confidently as if it had looked things up. Without tool results, the model doesn't know what happened in the last step and may call the same tool over and over. Delete an earlier call but keep its result and the next request doesn't connect: every tool result must match a call. Some providers reject such a request outright; others accept it, but the model may misread it.

what-is-agent.context-parts.paragraphs.2.text: This also draws the boundary of the model's knowledge: what isn't in the context doesn't exist for the model. A project file being on disk doesn't mean the model knows it; the model can see it only when the program reads it and puts it into the request. Some coding tools let you add a file to the conversation with a syntax like @, which is meant to put the file's content into the context. Claude Code reads the project's `CLAUDE.md` at the start of a session and puts the project conventions written there into the context, for the same reason. {{lesson:messages-context}} removes one of these parts at a time and compares how the answer changes.

what-is-agent.environment.paragraphs.0.text: An agent deals with the outside world through just two channels: observations come in, actions go out. The environment is the outside world the agent works in; for a coding agent, that is the project directory, terminal, tests, and clock. An observation is information the environment returns to the agent; an action is an operation the agent performs on the environment.

what-is-agent.environment.paragraphs.1.text: In an LLM agent, both channels run through tools. Reading files, searching code, and reading the clock are tools that obtain observations; editing files and running commands are tools that change the environment. After each action, the tool result is the new observation. It may be data or an error: file not found, command failed, permission denied. An error is an observation too, and the model relies on it to decide whether to try another way or stop.

what-is-agent.environment.paragraphs.2.text: The two channels also set the limits of what an agent can do. Information that never entered the context through an observation is unknown to the model; an operation that was never made into a tool stays at the level of a written suggestion, even if the model knows how to do it. Many problems that seem to need a smarter model are really interface problems: put the data you need in, make the operations you need into tools, and the task may become solvable.

what-is-agent.quiz-disk-file.disk-file.p.text: Your project files are on the same computer that runs the coding agent. Can the model directly know what is written in a given file?

what-is-agent.quiz-disk-file.disk-file.a.text: Yes, the file is right on the local machine
Not quite. Which computer the file is on doesn't matter. What matters is whether its content entered this request.

what-is-agent.quiz-disk-file.disk-file.b.text: Yes, as long as the system prompt gives the file path
Not enough. With only the path, the model just sees a string of text. A program has to read the file and put the content into the request.

what-is-agent.quiz-disk-file.disk-file.c.text: No, unless a program reads the file and puts the content into the context
Correct. What isn't in the context doesn't exist for the model.

what-is-agent.quiz-disk-file.disk-file.e.text: The model sees only what is in the request. Information on disk or in a database has to go through a tool or program to reach the context.

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.title.text: The autonomy spectrum: how much of the flow the model's output decides

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.paragrap.text: The more the model's output affects the program's flow, the more autonomous the system. This is a continuous spectrum; there is no clear line between "is an agent" and "is not an agent." Below are five levels from low to high, with examples taken from common software and scenarios.
Each level further down the table adds flexibility and adds more to check. Level 4 is the agent loop this course is about; level 5 is left for the multi-agent lessons.

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.0.1.text: Nothing; the output is only displayed or saved

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.0.2.text: A model translates a web page into English and the result is shown directly on the page

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.1.1.text: The program takes one of the branches written in advance, based on the model's judgment

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.1.2.text: A support system has the model judge whether a message is about "tracking a package" or "returns and exchanges," then routes it to the matching process

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.2.1.text: Which function to call and with which arguments

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.2.2.text: The model decides to call a "check weather" tool with the argument "Beijing"

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.3.1.text: After each step, the model decides whether to do one more step or finish

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.3.2.text: A coding agent runs the tests, reads the output, and then decides whether to keep editing or finish

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.4.1.text: One agent hands a subtask to another agent

what-is-agent.autonomy-spectrum.rows.4.2.text: A coding agent like Claude Code can hand a subtask such as "find all call sites in the codebase" to a subagent and wait for it to return the result

what-is-agent.quiz-autonomy-level.autono.text: Imagine a mailbox that has a model judge whether each new email is spam: if it is, the email goes to the spam folder; if not, it stays in the inbox. Which level of the autonomy spectrum is this?
More than that. The model's judgment decides where the email goes, which changes which path the program takes.
Correct. The model only classifies, and both paths are written in advance by the program.
Not this level. Each email is judged once, and the model can't decide to do another step.
Look at what the model's output controls: here it only decides which ready-made branch to take.

what-is-agent.cycle.title.text: Think, act, observe: a minimal loop

what-is-agent.cycle.paragraphs.0.text: The agent loop is three steps repeated. Think: the model decides the next step from the context. Act: it proposes a tool call, which the program executes. Observe: the result goes back into the context for the next round of thinking.

what-is-agent.cycle.paragraphs.1.text: Below, we walk through "read the current time and add the hour and the minute." The model has to get the real time first, because it will be the argument of the addition. This is an illustration of the mechanism; for the exact fields, go by the provider protocol and the real records in the Lab.

what-is-agent.cycle.item-1.text.text: The program sends the user's question, the definitions of the available tools, and the existing messages to the model.

what-is-agent.cycle.item-2.text.text: The model proposes a call to read the time. At this point there is only a tool call proposal; the clock has not been read yet.

what-is-agent.cycle.item-3.text.text: Python validates and executes the registered tool and gets the real time.

what-is-agent.cycle.item-4.text.text: The program puts the result, with the matching `tool_call_id`, into the next round of messages.

what-is-agent.cycle.item-5.text.text: Based on the actual time, the model proposes an addition call; the program executes it and sends the result back.

what-is-agent.cycle.item-6.text.text: The model gives an answer, or the program stops because of an error, a cancellation, or reaching the round limit.

what-is-agent.agent-loop.title.text: One minimal loop, walked through on the stage

what-is-agent.agent-loop.caption.text: This is an illustration: the events are authored to explain the structure. Your own runs light up the same stage with real events in the Lab scene.

what-is-agent.stop-conditions.paragraphs.text: The loop must have a stop condition. Otherwise a run might never end, and the cost has no ceiling. The most natural stop is the model no longer proposing calls and giving an answer directly. But the model may also keep calling: when fixing a bug the test keeps failing and it edits and reruns again and again, or it always feels it needs to look up a bit more.

So the harness sets up other gates: stop at the round limit; stop on an unrecoverable error, such as a tool that doesn't exist or arguments that can't be repaired; stop when the user clicks stop; stop when the budget runs out. Every way of stopping must record its reason in the run's terminal state. {{lesson:tool-selection}} gives the loop a round limit, and {{lesson:fail-safely}} looks at how to stop safely when something goes wrong.

The loop stopping and the task being done are separate things. The model no longer calling tools only means it thinks it can answer; whether the answer meets the requirements must be checked separately against acceptance criteria. The next chapter returns to this.

what-is-agent.claude-code-bugfix.title.text: Taking apart one Claude Code bug fix

what-is-agent.claude-code-bugfix.paragra.text: Every step of Claude Code fixing a bug maps onto the four positions above and onto the think, act, observe loop. Below is a made-up run. It describes only behavior you can see in the interface while using it; what you see depends on the product. How it is implemented internally is not guessed at here.

Two things show in the table. The model is responsible only for proposing the next step; execution, confirmation, and recording all happen in the harness. The loop stops because the model no longer proposes operations; whether the task is done is for you to judge from the test output and the changes.

what-is-agent.claude-code-bugfix.columns.text: What you see in the interface

what-is-agent.claude-code-bugfix.rows.0..text: You type "the login test is failing, fix it"
Your task and the project conventions in `CLAUDE.md` enter the context, and the definitions of the available tools are in it too

what-is-agent.claude-code-bugfix.rows.1..text: It says it will look at the test and the error first, and a file-read operation appears in the log
The model proposes a call to read a file, the harness executes it, and the file content goes back to the model as a tool result

what-is-agent.claude-code-bugfix.rows.2..text: It proposes changing a condition, shows a diff of the change, and waits for your confirmation
The model proposes an edit; according to the permission settings, the harness stops to ask you, and changes the file in the environment only after you agree

what-is-agent.claude-code-bugfix.rows.3..text: It runs the tests, and one failure is still in the output
The test output is a new observation and goes back into the context; the model uses it to decide to keep editing

what-is-agent.claude-code-bugfix.rows.4..text: It fixes one more place, reruns, all tests pass, and it writes a summary
The model no longer proposes operations, and the loop stops on its own

what-is-agent.claude-code-bugfix.rows.5..text: You look at the test output and the diff and decide whether to accept
Acceptance is outside the loop; you or a program judge it against criteria

what-is-agent.quiz-claude-code-stop.clau.text: After running the tests, Claude Code stops proposing new operations and replies "fixed." Which judgment is correct?
The loop stopped, so the task must be done
Not quite. The loop stopping only means the model no longer proposes operations. Whether the task is done depends on the test output and the changes.
The model stopped proposing calls, so the loop stopped naturally; whether it is fixed depends on the test output and the changes
Correct. The stop condition governs when the loop stops; acceptance governs whether the result is right.
It must have hit the round limit
No basis for that. When the round limit is hit, the harness records that reason; here the model gave an answer itself.
Stopping and being done are two different things: the former depends on the terminal state and its reason, the latter on acceptance criteria and evidence.

what-is-agent.tool-call-four-steps.title.text: The four steps of a tool call, across providers

what-is-agent.tool-call-four-steps.summa.text: Declare, propose, execute and return, answer: the four steps stay the same, and the field names differ by provider.

what-is-agent.tool-call-four-steps.parag.text: Break a tool call apart and nearly every provider uses four steps. One: the request declares which tools exist, with name, purpose, and parameter structure. Two: the model decides whether to call, which one, and with which arguments, and writes a tool call proposal in the response. Three: the program executes it and puts the result into the next request. Four: the model reads the result and decides whether to keep calling or to answer.

The difference is in the field names. In the compatible format this platform uses, a response whose `finish_reason` is `tool_calls` means the model wants to call a tool, the proposal is in `tool_calls`, and the result is sent back as a message whose `role` is `tool`, matched to the proposal by `tool_call_id`. Some providers use another set of names, for example a `stop_reason` of `tool_use` to mean a tool call is wanted, with the result placed in a dedicated block inside a user message. The names differ; the division of labor in the four steps is the same.

The simplest example is a calculator. A model is prone to errors when multiplying big numbers in its head, as the previous chapter said. Give it a multiplication tool and it only has to propose "use the multiplication tool on these two numbers"; the program computes exactly and hands the result back. The model decides what to do and the program makes sure it is done correctly. That is the plainest use of a tool.

what-is-agent.thought-is-not-evidence.cl.text: The model wrote "I've run the tests and they all pass" in its answer, so it did run them.

what-is-agent.thought-is-not-evidence.co.text: That sentence, like any other part of the answer, is text the model generated. Whether the tests ran depends only on whether the record contains the matching command call and its output. The thoughts and plans the model writes can help you understand its intent, but they are not evidence of action.

what-is-agent.memory.title.text: Message history, application state, and persistent memory are not the same thing

what-is-agent.memory.paragraphs.0.text: Message history is the sequence of messages the program sends with each request. Application state is structured data the program maintains, such as the current step and the tasks completed. Persistent memory is information saved across runs and retrieved when needed. They may refer to one another, but they are not the same thing.

what-is-agent.memory.paragraphs.1.text: Adding tool results to the next round's request changes what the model sees this time; it doesn't update the model's parameters. Saving preferences doesn't automatically bring reliable "self-learning" either: what to save, when to retrieve it, and how to verify the effect all have to be designed explicitly. {{lesson:application-state}} and {{lesson:persistent-memory}} deal with the latter two respectively.

workflow-or-agent.summary.text: A single call, a workflow, and an agent each have their uses: first ask who decides the next step, then weigh cost, latency, and controllability.

workflow-or-agent.next_label.text: Last: learning path and lab bench

workflow-or-agent.objectives.objective-1.text: Say how a single call, a workflow, and an agent differ: who decides the next step.

workflow-or-agent.objectives.objective-2.text: Choose a form for a requirement using three yardsticks: cost, latency, and controllability.

workflow-or-agent.objectives.objective-3.text: Recognize common workflow shapes such as prompt chaining, routing, and parallelization.

workflow-or-agent.objectives.objective-4.text: Explain why "giving an answer" and "passing the task's acceptance check" are two different things.

workflow-or-agent.simplest-first.title.text: From a single call to an agent: start with the simplest option

workflow-or-agent.simplest-first.paragra.text: If one model call solves it, don't build a workflow; if a workflow solves it, don't build an agent. This is a rule of thumb often cited when building LLM applications. The agent loop from the previous chapter is flexible, at the price of more model calls, longer waits, and less predictable behavior.

The three levels differ in one question: who decides the next step. A single call has no next step; it is one question and one answer. In a workflow, the steps and branches are written in advance by the program, and the model only produces the content inside each step. In an agent, the model decides the steps at run time, looking at the result of the previous step before choosing the next.

Many processes you meet in daily life are written in advance. Expense approval goes through submission, verification, approval, and payment in order. A parcel sorting line sends each package to the matching chute by the address on the label. A support hotline follows a menu: "press 1 to track a package, press 2 for returns and exchanges," and transfers you to a person if no option fits. These steps can be written down beforehand, and a program orchestrating them is more reliable. Asking a coding agent to fix a bug with an unknown cause is different: which files to read, which places to change, and how many times to run the tests can't be said beforehand. That is when an agent's turn comes.

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.title.text: Three levels side by side: who decides the next step

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.paragraph.text: The same kind of need can be more or less open-ended, and the suitable form changes with it. Here are three examples side by side.

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.rows.0.2.text: Ask a chat app to explain an error message

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.rows.0.3.text: The input is all the information, and one answer is enough

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.rows.1.1.text: Steps and branches the program wrote in advance

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.rows.1.2.text: An expense system: upload a photo of the invoice, the model reads the amount and date, the program checks the expense limit, then finds the approver by amount

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.rows.1.3.text: Tasks with fixed steps that can be written down in advance

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.rows.2.1.text: The model decides at run time, based on observations

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.rows.2.2.text: A coding agent fixing a bug with an unknown cause: look at the error first, then decide which file to read, which lines to change, and which tests to run, based on what it finds

workflow-or-agent.three-levels.rows.2.3.text: Open-ended tasks where the number and order of steps can't be said in advance

workflow-or-agent.workflow-shapes.paragr.text: Workflows are put together from a few common shapes. In all of them the program controls the flow and the model only works inside the nodes. Recognizing these shapes helps you judge whether a requirement really needs an agent. For the first three, the steps are already fixed when you write the code.

Prompt chaining: split a task into a few steps in a fixed order, where the output of one step is the input of the next, and you can put gates between steps. For example, an expense system first reads the invoice, then checks the amount, and finally generates an approval summary. Routing: first have the model classify the input, then the program hands it to different flows. It is like the support menu's "press 1, press 2," except the user can describe the problem in their own words and the model decides which branch to take. Parallelization: send independent subtasks out at the same time and have the program combine the results, for example handing five clauses of a contract to the model to check separately.

Two more complex ones. Orchestrator-workers: one model splits the task into subtasks and hands them to several workers, and the program collects the results and checks the format. Unlike parallelization, the subtasks are split out at run time: when a requirement changes several files, which ones and how many parts you only know after reading the code. Evaluator-optimizer: one role generates, another reviews against criteria and gives comments, and they loop through revisions until the output passes or the iteration limit is reached; for example, one role translates and another picks out errors against a glossary. {{lesson:workflow-patterns}} and {{lesson:orchestrator-evaluator}} build each of these shapes once.

workflow-or-agent.quiz-which-shape.which.text: An online support system has the model first judge whether your message is about "tracking a package," "returns and exchanges," or a "complaint," then hands it to a process written in advance, and complaints go straight to a person. Which shape is this?
Not quite. The steps of a prompt chain follow a fixed order and don't switch paths depending on the input.
Correct. The model only classifies, and the process for each category is written in advance by the program.
Not quite. After classification, the path is already settled, and the model can't decide to add another step.
The key to routing: the model's output only decides which ready-made path to take.

workflow-or-agent.tradeoffs.title.text: Cost, latency, and controllability: three yardsticks

workflow-or-agent.tradeoffs.paragraphs.0.text: What an agent buys is flexibility, and what it pays is cost, latency, and controllability. Start with cost: an agent makes another model request at every step, and each time it resends an ever-longer message history. For a task that takes eight rounds, there are eight model calls, and input tokens add up across the rounds. A workflow's number of model calls is either fixed or has a clear upper bound, so you can estimate the most it will cost in advance.

workflow-or-agent.tradeoffs.paragraphs.1.text: Now latency. Each round has to wait for the model to finish writing and for the tools to finish executing before the next round can start, and the waiting stacks up round by round. A made-up example: at an average of 4 seconds per round, eight rounds is over half a minute. In a workflow, independent steps can run in parallel, and the total wait depends on the slowest path.

workflow-or-agent.tradeoffs.paragraphs.2.text: Finally, controllability. A workflow's path is hard-coded, so you can test it case by case, and a rule like "payment requires approval first" is guaranteed by the program. An agent's path may differ every time: on the same task it may check three times now and five times next time, so the tests have to cover many more cases, and once it takes a wrong step, the later steps build on the error. In return, when it meets a situation nobody anticipated, it can find its own way.

workflow-or-agent.compound-errors.summar.text: Every step may be reliable and the chain still not be; work out the success rate of a multi-step task by hand.

workflow-or-agent.compound-errors.paragr.text: Suppose an agent gets each step right with probability 0.9. This number is made up, just for the demonstration. For a one-step task, the success rate is 0.9. A five-step task needs every step to be right, so the success rate is `0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 ≈ 0.59`, and about four in ten runs go wrong at some step. Ten steps gives `0.9^10 ≈ 0.35`.

So the longer an agent runs, the more likely something goes wrong. A workflow also accumulates errors, but it can put gates between steps. For example, after reading an invoice, the program checks the format of the amount and date, and stops or redoes the step if the check fails, so a bad result is not passed on. As long as the gate catches most errors, the later steps build on results that passed.

An agent can borrow the idea too: make tool results structured data a program can check; add verification after key steps; return a clear error when something fails, so the model has a chance to correct itself. These measures can't raise the success rate to 100%, but they let an error be caught at the step where it happens, instead of surfacing only in the final answer.

workflow-or-agent.quiz-invoice-steps.inv.text: An expense system processes an invoice. The workflow version makes a fixed 3 model calls (read the amount, read the date, write the summary). After switching to an agent version, it averages 7 rounds. Which statement is the most accurate?
The agent version is better, because it calls the model more times
More calls doesn't mean better results. Compare the two against acceptance criteria, then see whether the extra calls are worth it.
This task has fixed steps, so a workflow is cheaper, faster, and easier to test
Correct. When the steps can be written down in advance, the agent's flexibility goes unused, and all you get extra is cost and uncertainty.
The costs are the same, because it is the same model
Not quite. Cost grows with the number of model calls and the number of tokens sent each time, and with the same model it can still differ a lot.
To choose a form, first ask whether the steps can be written down in advance; if they can, let the program control the flow.

workflow-or-agent.reimbursement-vs-bugfi.text: Two examples: expense approval and fixing an open-ended bug

Put a fixed process next to an open-ended task and the difference is clearest. The rules of expense approval are written out in full; with a bug of unknown cause, you don't even know in advance which files to look at.
Dimension
Expense approval
Having a coding agent fix a bug
Can the steps be written down in advance
Yes: verify the invoice, check the amount limit, find the approver by amount, notify the result
No: you know which file to read only after seeing the error, and the next step only after running the tests following a change
Where the rules come from
Company policy, written as conditions in the program
There are no ready-made rules; the model judges from the error and the code
Cost of an error
High: an over-claim or a missed approval causes real loss
Depends on permissions: if it only changes the local workspace and there is version control, it can be undone; if it can delete files or push code, the cost is high
What the model is good for
Only work that is hard to write out as rules, inside a node, such as reading the amount from an invoice photo
Deciding which file to read, which lines to change, and which tests to run, and how to explain the change to you
How to check acceptance
The program checks the amount, approver, and status against the rules, one by one
Criteria written in advance, such as "the test that failed now passes and no other test newly fails"
Recommended form
A workflow, with human approval at key nodes
An agent loop, with a round limit, a command scope, and acceptance criteria set up

workflow-or-agent.answer-is-not-acceptan.text: Giving an answer is not the same as passing the acceptance check

When an agent stops and gives an answer, it only shows that the model thinks it can finish, not that the task is really done. Imagine a coding agent ends with: "Fixed, all tests pass." In reality it may have run only some of the tests; it may have changed the tests themselves to make them pass; it may have fixed this bug and broken something else; or it may not have run the tests at all.

The reason is in the previous chapter: the most natural stop condition for the loop is the model no longer proposing calls. That is the model's own judgment, and like "I've already run it," it is a piece of output, not evidence. The stronger the model, the more convincing this self-declared completion looks, and the more it needs an external check.

So "finished" has to be split into at least four judgments: did the run enter a terminal state normally; does the task result meet the acceptance criteria agreed in advance; do the conclusions come with evidence from this run's observations; did the process stay within the allowed scope. The four are independent of each other, and the next chapter covers them in more detail. {{lesson:task-contract}} teaches you to write acceptance criteria before you start; {{lesson:reflection-revision}} compares the model's self-assessment with a review based on real test results.

workflow-or-agent.agent-is-better.claim.text: An agent is more advanced than a workflow, so use an agent whenever you can.

workflow-or-agent.agent-is-better.correc.text: Pick the form by the task, not by which sounds more advanced. For tasks whose steps can be written down in advance, a workflow is cheaper, faster, and easier to test. Only for open-ended tasks whose steps can't be stated is the agent's flexibility worth the extra calls and extra uncertainty.

workflow-or-agent.mixing.title.text: Mixing: a fixed skeleton with local delegation

workflow-or-agent.mixing.paragraphs.0.text: Real systems rarely use just one form. A common approach is a fixed skeleton with delegation in places. The expense system as a whole is a workflow, but the "read the invoice" step can be handed to a small agent that tries another way by itself when the photo is unclear. Conversely, a coding agent as a whole is a loop, but for actions with side effects, such as deleting files or pushing code, you put a gate in front that requires your confirmation.

workflow-or-agent.mixing.paragraphs.1.text: What to fix and what to delegate? A practical criterion is how clear the rules are and how costly an error is. Where the rules are clear and an error is costly, such as permissions, amounts, deletion, and sending things out, the program fixes it. Where the rules are hard to state and an error can be recovered, such as what to look up and how to organize an explanation, leave it to the model.

workflow-or-agent.mixing.paragraphs.2.text: This line moves as models change. The stronger the model, the more can be delegated, and something that used to be split into several steps by the program may now be done in one call. So revisit the fixed parts from time to time: are they still preventing real errors, or just constraining a model that can already do the job? The basis for the judgment is still a controlled experiment.

workflow-or-agent.two-views.title.text: Two views: start simple, or trust the model

workflow-or-agent.two-views.summary.text: One camp stresses workflows first; the other stresses not binding the model with a flowchart. They are about different tasks.

workflow-or-agent.two-views.paragraphs.0.text: On workflows and agents, you often see two claims that sound opposite. One comes from a summary of engineering practice: start with the simplest option, use a fixed flow whenever you can, and let the model decide the steps only when truly necessary. The other comes from people who build coding agents: the ability to act comes from model training, and stuffing the model into a hard-coded flowchart treats it as a fancy text-completion node and makes the system fragile.

workflow-or-agent.two-views.paragraphs.1.text: The two claims are about different tasks. The former mostly deals with business processes that have clear steps: support triage, document extraction, expense approval. There a fixed flow really is cheaper and steadier. The latter deals with open-ended tasks like coding: which files to read, which places to change, and how many times to run the tests can't be written out in advance, and forcing a flow onto them only hits walls everywhere.

workflow-or-agent.two-views.paragraphs.2.text: The two claims also have something in common: neither lets the model directly hold permissions, and both require the harness to provide clear tools, context, and checks. The only difference is who gets control of the flow. When you read this kind of debate, first ask whether the steps of the task can be written down in advance.

learning-path-lab.route.title.text: The learning path: the harness grows layer by layer

learning-path-lab.route.paragraphs.0.text: The learning path builds up by capability, and each unit adds one thing to the harness. The syllabus in the sidebar is organized by category, module, and lesson. Available lessons come with a full explanation and experiments; the grayed-out planned lessons only show the direction and can't be run yet. For the current number of available lessons, see the course catalog.

learning-path-lab.route.paragraphs.1.text: The existing foundation experiments start with the single model request in {{lesson:chat-request}}, then in turn look at multi-turn conversation, sampling, the proposal and execution of tool calls, dependent multi-round calls, and error handling and boundaries. Later units build on the same native mechanisms, instead of switching to a new demo each time a framework appears.

learning-path-lab.route.item-1.text.text: Native foundations: send a request, propose a call, execute a tool, return the result, stop safely. The program grows from one question and one answer into a minimal agent loop.

learning-path-lab.route.item-2.text.text: Tasks and interfaces: write acceptance criteria first, then constrain the model with structured output and tool descriptions. What the program hands over can be checked.

learning-path-lab.route.item-3.text.text: Context and state: the message protocol, application state, context budget and compression, persistent memory, prompt caching. The program remembers, fits within the window, and doesn't lose things across runs.

learning-path-lab.route.item-4.text.text: Reasoning and control patterns: text actions, TODO lists, plan-and-execute, reflection and revision, workflow patterns. The program can schedule multi-step tasks.

learning-path-lab.route.item-5.text.text: Knowledge and retrieval (planned): chunking, retrieval, and answers with cited sources. An answer can point to where it came from.

learning-path-lab.route.item-6.text.text: Frameworks and orchestration (planned): implement the same task with LangChain and LangGraph, compare it with the native implementation, then add approval, human-in-the-loop, and resumption.

learning-path-lab.route.item-7.text.text: Coding agents, quality and reliability, protocols and tool services (planned): execution environments, evaluation sets, observability, reliable tools, prompt injection, MCP.

learning-path-lab.route.item-8.text.text: Capstone projects (planned): division of labor among multiple agents, long-running tasks, and finally delivering a local coding assistant or learning assistant.

learning-path-lab.setup.paragraphs.0.text: Reading the intro chapters, browsing the course material, and doing the end-of-chapter checks all send no model request. Before starting real experiments, confirm the provider, model, and credentials in the model connection settings; the model must support the tool calling the course uses. Every call to a remote service generates actual usage with that provider.

learning-path-lab.setup.paragraphs.1.text: Some exercises don't call a model at all, such as {{lesson:task-contract}}, {{lesson:application-state}}, and some fault-injection exercises. They are executed by the local runner and need no model connection, and the lab area marks them "Run locally". All other exercises are real runs, and when no model is available, the page first guides you through the setup.

learning-path-lab.setup.paragraphs.2.text: Tools run in local Python, and the web page shows the material and the run record. The code area shows real files the course allows to be public, read-only. To change code, edit it in a local editor and restart the service as the project instructions say. Old commands, model names, and cloud platform requirements in the reference tutorials apply only to their own examples; you don't need to copy them.

learning-path-lab.first-run.title.text: For your first run, check along this chain of evidence

learning-path-lab.first-run.paragraphs.0.text: If you have used a coding agent, you have seen it list, one by one in the terminal or a side panel, which file it read, which command it ran, and what the command printed. The run console on the lab bench is the same kind of record, with one more layer: each request sent to the model and each response from the model. Go into {{lesson:chat-request}}, run the "With system prompt" exercise, and then check along the chain below. What is listed here is the structure you should look for; it doesn't guarantee the model uses any particular wording. If it takes a different path, explain the difference from the real record.

learning-path-lab.first-run.item-1.text.text: In the event that sends the request, find the message list: the rules in `system` and your question, and confirm what the model could see this time.

learning-path-lab.first-run.item-2.text.text: In the event for the model's response, find the answer content and the finish reason, `finish_reason`.

learning-path-lab.first-run.item-3.text.text: In the usage, read how many tokens went in and out; for any item the provider did not report, record it as not reported.

learning-path-lab.first-run.item-4.text.text: In the tool lessons, use the same method to find `tool_calls`, the tool call and tool result events, and then in the next round's request find the message whose `role` is `tool` and its matching `tool_call_id`.

learning-path-lab.sdk-vs-raw.title.text: How raw bodies differ from SDK-standardized data

learning-path-lab.sdk-vs-raw.summary.text: The Bailian path shows raw HTTP bodies; other providers show SDK-standardized data. What each can prove is different.

learning-path-lab.sdk-vs-raw.paragraphs..text: The platform connects to models in two ways. Bailian uses the course's hand-written raw HTTP path, and the record shows the request body this path actually sent and the response body it actually received. Other providers are called through a unified client library, which converts each provider's different format into one common structure. The record shows the request and response after conversion, and the interface labels them "SDK-standardized".

SDK-standardized data is easier to compare: different providers' answers, calls, and usage sit in the same fields. But it is not the raw message transmitted over the wire. Conversion may omit provider-specific fields, and the library may also do other things internally, which are not necessarily reflected in the record. This platform has turned off the library's automatic retries.

So when you cite evidence, say where it came from: "`tool_calls` in the SDK-standardized response" and "`tool_calls` in the HTTP response body" are two different statements. The former is enough to tell what call the model proposed; to study the protocol details of a particular provider, you need the raw body.

learning-path-lab.playback.title.text: Replay doesn't call the model again

learning-path-lab.playback.paragraphs.0.text: A run sends real model requests and executes the course's tools; a replay only moves a cursor among events that have already been received. You can pause and step forward and back through the same record to check where the arguments came from. A replay does not re-read the time and does not recompute anything. To compare a different input, explicitly start a new run.

learning-path-lab.playback.paragraphs.1.text: There is another case that is easy to confuse with replay: when the question, arguments, prompt, and code are all unchanged, the lab bench shows your previous run directly and notes that it did not request the model again. This avoids paying again for the same input; for a fresh result, run it again.

learning-path-lab.playback.paragraphs.2.text: Clicking Stop asks the backend to stop the rest of the flow. An upstream network request that has already been sent may still wait for a response or a timeout, so don't take the interface no longer updating to mean the backend has finished. Use the terminal state and error information in the record to decide whether you can start the next run.

learning-path-lab.quiz-replay-is-read-on.text: In a replay you drag the progress back to round 2, then step forward. What does the platform do?
Requests the model again to see whether it gives a different answer this time
Not quite. Replay sends no model request.
Re-executes the round 2 tool to refresh the tool result
Not quite. The tool result was recorded at the time, and replay doesn't execute tools again.
Only moves among the recorded events and shows the request, response, and result from that time
Correct. Replay is read-only; to get a new result you have to start a new run.
A run produces new events; a replay only reads old events.

learning-path-lab.trace-boundary.title.text: What a record can prove, and where it stops

learning-path-lab.trace-boundary.paragra.text: The glow, timing, and status animations in the interface help you see progress; they can't prove what thinking went on inside the model. A tool call is an external action you can inspect; a plan or explanation the model states about itself should be read separately from the actual events.

When usage is not returned, the report shows "not reported"; a missing field must not be taken as zero. While waiting for the model, the interface shows only real timing, and does not use text like "thinking" to stand in for a process you can't see.

learning-path-lab.validate.paragraphs.0.text: When a run ends, check at least four things separately. With division by zero, the correct behavior may be the tool returning a structured error and the model explaining the limit to the user; making up a number does not count as success, however confident the tone. Conversely, a final value that happens to be correct doesn't prove the required tool was used.

learning-path-lab.validate.columns.2.text: Example: a coding agent fixing a bug

learning-path-lab.validate.rows.0.1.text: Whether normal completion, failure, or cancellation is clearly recorded

learning-path-lab.validate.rows.0.2.text: The record has an end event, and the terminal state and its reason are clear

learning-path-lab.validate.rows.1.1.text: Whether the answer meets the acceptance criteria agreed in advance for this problem

learning-path-lab.validate.rows.1.2.text: The test that failed now passes, and no other test newly fails

learning-path-lab.validate.rows.2.1.text: Whether the conclusion and arguments come from this run's actual observations

learning-path-lab.validate.rows.2.2.text: "All tests pass" can be found in the output of the command that ran the tests

learning-path-lab.validate.rows.3.1.text: Whether the tools, arguments, number of calls, and scope of operations stayed within what is allowed

learning-path-lab.validate.rows.3.2.text: Only the allowed commands were run, and no files outside the agreed scope were changed

learning-path-lab.finished-means-passed..text: The lab bench shows "Completed", so this experiment passed.

"Completed" means the run entered a terminal state normally, which is only the first of the four judgments. Whether the answer meets the acceptance criteria, whether the conclusion has evidence, and whether the process stayed within bounds each have to be checked separately.

learning-path-lab.first-week.title.text: How to study in the first week

learning-path-lab.first-week.paragraphs..text: The goal for the first week is to be able to explain one run completely. One focused session can aim for just one small goal: read the Understand scene, write down a prediction, run a preset exercise, gather all the evidence, and do one check.

Next time, change only one factor, for example keep the model and tools the same and change only the numbers in the question. Once you can explain why the behavior changed, move on to comparing models, prompts, or frameworks. Planned lessons have no experiments yet. You can read the matching concepts from the references as optional reading, but don't treat optional reading as a platform experiment that has already passed.

Before each session ends, leave one verifiable conclusion in your learner notes: "Which round's response proposed which call, what it actually returned, how the next round used it, and so which criterion this run passed or failed." In later, more complex projects, use the same method to build a fixed question set, so you can tell whether a change brought an improvement or a regression.

learning-path-lab.one-run-one-sample.tit.text: One run is just one sample

learning-path-lab.one-run-one-sample.sum.text: To conclude that "this change helps," hold the other conditions fixed, change one thing, and run several times.

learning-path-lab.one-run-one-sample.par.text: Model output is random, so one run can only tell you what happened this time. You changed one line of a tool description and the model picked the right tool this time. That may be the description working, or it may be just luck of the draw.

A more reliable approach has three parts: fix the model, the question, and the budget, and change only the one thing you are studying; run each arm several times and look at the distribution of results, instead of picking the best run; put the records of the two arms side by side and judge them by the same criterion. This is a controlled experiment, and {{lesson:sampling-variance}} and {{lesson:prompt-experiments}} will take you through it.

There is no single answer to how many runs are enough; it depends on how far apart the two arms are and how much they fluctuate. When the difference is large, a few runs show it; when it is small, you need more samples, or you have to admit the evidence isn't enough to conclude anything. The platform's lab report lists each run's check results so you can compare them.
